title: True Practice, Real Awakening
author: Annotated by Zhanran
excerpt: In studying the Buddha's way, what matters is true practice and real awakening, so as to be free of birth and death. Not letting a single thought slip by is true practice; passing through each thought unobstructed is real awakening.

inline.s: Not letting a single thought slip by; passing through each thought unobstructed.
In studying the Buddha's way, what matters is true practice and real awakening,
so as to be free of birth and death
. Not letting a single thought slip by is true practice; passing through each thought unobstructed is real awakening.

[not letting it slip by] not being deceived or concealed by it. [passing through it] not being enveloped by it, not following or being toyed with by it, not treating it as a real thing, and still less being taken hostage by it.

Studying the Buddha's way is only a matter of finding an ultimate way out at the pass of birth and death — not of seeking, apart from this, some strange and extraordinary matter in the words and ink of the scriptures or in the twelve divisions of the Three Vehicles.
In daily life, not departing from any dharma and not dwelling on any dharma, letting nothing slip by anywhere and passing through each thing unobstructed — this is true, genuine practice.
On this point, Master Hanshan Deqing, in his Mengyou ji,
"Instruction to Dharma Master Miaozhan," gives a penetrating teaching, which I here excerpt and annotate as follows:

From of old, when people left home it was for the great matter of birth and death. Even the Buddhas and patriarchs appeared in the world only to reveal and instruct in this matter. Apart from birth and death there is no Buddhadharma, and apart from the Buddhadharma there is no birth and death. As it is said, when one is deluded, birth and death begin; when one awakens, the cycle of rebirth ceases. From this we know that the ancients' seeking and inquiry lay only in finding the ultimate resolution at the pass of birth and death — not in seeking, apart from this, some strange and extraordinary matter in the words and ink of the scriptures or in the twelve divisions of the Three Vehicles.

From of old, when the ancients left home it was for the great matter of freeing themselves from birth and death. Even when the Buddhas and patriarchs appeared in the world, it was specifically to reveal and instruct in this matter (freedom from birth and death) and nothing else. There is no Buddhadharma apart from this great matter of freedom from birth and death, nor is there any freedom from birth and death apart from the Buddhadharma. (This is to say: the Buddhadharma is precisely the freeing of oneself from birth and death, and only that which frees one from birth and death is the Buddhadharma. Here "birth and death" refers to birth and death in stages and birth and death of transformation.) As it is said, when one is deluded, birth and death begin; when one awakens, the cycle of rebirth ceases. ("The cycle of rebirth ceases" means freedom from birth and death in stages. Here Master Hanshan especially emphasizes freedom from birth and death in stages, because this is the urgent task of the practitioner.) From this we know that the ancients' seeking and inquiry lay only in finding an ultimate way out at the pass of birth and death, and not in seeking, apart from this, any strange and extraordinary matter in the words and ink of the scriptures or in the twelve divisions of the Three Vehicles.

[birth and death in stages] For beings in the three realms and six paths, on account of the ripening of good and evil karma, their lifespans all have their limits and their bodily forms all have their distinctions, and therefore their birth and death is called "birth and death in stages." To be free of birth and death in stages is to escape the cycle of rebirth. [birth and death of transformation] The sages of the Three Vehicles have already cut off the delusions of views and thought and are free of birth and death in stages. In the course of their cultivation of the Way, deluded thoughts gradually die away and realization gradually increases. Each stage of this migration between delusion and awakening differs from the next, and the movement from an earlier stage to a later one is like a birth and death in itself; its transformations are wondrous and unfathomable, beyond conception, and hence it is called "birth and death of transformation." To be free of birth and death of transformation is to perfectly realize the fruit of Buddhahood.

Therefore Bodhidharma came from the West and set up no written words, seeking only the awakening and penetration of one's own mind — for this mind is the root of all sages and ordinary beings and of the proper and dependent rewards of the ten realms. To fully awaken to this mind is to be the supreme sage of the Mahāyāna; to awaken to it in part is to be of the Two Vehicles; not to awaken to it is to be an ordinary being. And to awaken yet not cling to the awakening, to realize yet not regard it as something attained — this is the single road that goes upward, beyond sage and ordinary being, beyond birth and death.

Therefore Patriarch Bodhidharma came from India (ancient Tianzhu) and established his principle: set up no written words, point directly at the human mind. Cultivation lies only in the awakening and penetration of one's own mind, because this mind is the root of all sages and ordinary beings and of the proper and dependent rewards of the ten dharma-realms. To fully awaken to this mind is to be the supreme sage of the Mahāyāna; to awaken to it in part is to be of the Two Vehicles; not to awaken to it is to be an ordinary being. And to awaken yet not cling to it in the mind, to realize yet not regard it as something attained — this is the single road that goes upward, beyond sage and ordinary being, beyond birth and death.

[the single road upward] The utmost point of the Chan school (beyond sage and ordinary being, beyond birth and death) is called "the single road upward." It has the same meaning as "the one step upward." Master Hanshan says:

"The essential purport of the Buddhist teaching is simply to take the one mind as the principle. This mind, in its origin, is perfectly complete, bright, vast, and great, entirely free of the finest dust, pure and empty of things. In it there is fundamentally no delusion or awakening, no birth or death; sage and ordinary being are not established, and living beings and Buddha are one in substance, without duality or difference. This is precisely what Bodhidharma, coming from the West, pointed to directly — this originally existing true mind — making it the Chan school. Therefore, when he faced Emperor Wu
(Emperor Wu of Liang)

he said: 'Vast emptiness, nothing holy.' If one can suddenly awaken to this mind, then birth and death are forever cut off. It lies only in the person's sudden awakening in a single thought, and one is then called the thusness Buddha. It does not belong to stages and ranks of cultivation and realization, nor to the gradual steps of the Three Vehicles. This the Chan school regards as the single road upward. What the patriarchs of old transmitted was simply this mind, taking it as the ultimate principle — and this is called Chan."
(Mengyou ji, "Reply to Prince De's Question") [vast emptiness] Here "vast emptiness" means: the appearance of empty stillness.

In recent times, students of the Way have grown ever more distant from the sages. They do not see how the ancients truly conducted themselves — passing through, one by one, the present circumstances of daily life and the shore of birth and death. In this very daily life, not departing from any dharma and not dwelling on any dharma, never lightly letting anything slip by — this is true, genuine practice. In all the present realms of form and sound, of adversity and ease, of love and hate, wherever one passes through unobstructed — this is the true gate of awakening. In this very awakening, each matter and each dharma is the true Buddhadharma. It is not that only when one listens to a teacher, when the bell is struck and the drum beaten and one ascends the lotus seat, opening wide one's mouth to imitate the cry of the wild jackal, cocking the ear, bowing the head, closing the eyes, and draping the robe, is there Buddhadharma. Therefore the youth Sudhana traveled south through a hundred cities, visiting and honoring good spiritual friends countless as the motes of dust in the Buddha-lands, and thus attained the awakening of the many gates of liberation, in every mote of dust and every land.

In recent times, students of the Way are distant from the sages and have not seen the true conduct of the ancients — passing through, one by one, the present circumstances of daily life and the shore of birth and death. This is to say: in daily life, not departing from (not avoiding) any dharma and not dwelling on (not clinging to) any dharma, never lightly letting anything slip by — this is true, genuine practice. In all the present realms of form and sound, of adversity and ease, of love and hate, wherever one passes through unobstructed (not being deluded by them, not being turned by them) — this is the true gate of awakening. In this very awakening, each thing and each matter is the true Buddhadharma. It is not that only when one listens to a lecturer of the scriptures — who strikes the bell, beats the drum, and ascends the Dharma seat, opening wide his mouth to imitate the cry of the wild jackal (falsely proclaiming the truth), cocking the ear, bowing the head, closing the eyes, and draping the robe (the gestures by which a teacher guides and awakens students) — is there Buddhadharma. Therefore the youth Sudhana journeyed south, passing through more than a hundred cities, visiting and honoring good spiritual friends countless as the motes of dust in the Buddha-lands, and in his practice realized the many gates of liberation in every mote of dust and every land.

[passing through unobstructed] not being entangled or manipulated by the sense-objects. [each matter] every single thing, every single item. [teacher] one who expounds the scriptures and teachings. [lotus seat] the lotus throne — here it refers to the Dharma seat from which the scriptures are expounded. [wild jackal] a kind of fox. "The cry of the wild jackal" is the counterpart of "the lion's roar," used as a metaphor for one whose practice is not yet mature yet who falsely proclaims the truth. [countless as the motes of dust in the Buddha-lands] a description of an extremely great number. [in every mote of dust and every land] the realm described in the Avatamsaka Sutra: within each and every mote of dust there appear countless Buddha-lands, and within each Buddha-land there are again countless motes of dust, within each of which again appear countless Buddha-lands, endlessly and inexhaustibly. Here "in every mote of dust and every land" is used to describe an extremely great number.

Now, setting aside the Dharma gates for the moment, even of good spiritual friends, how could there be so many as the motes of dust in the Buddha-lands? Little do people realize that "in every mote of dust and every land" refers to the deluded thoughts, cogitations, and emotional defilements of our own daily life. If, in daily life, at the place where thoughts arise, where the roots of passion are firmly knotted, where love and hate intertwine and are hard to untangle, and where the various habits of greed, anger, folly, and pride are hard to wear away — if right there, at the fundamental point of pain, you thrust
(here "zha" is the same as "zha")

an awl, piercing through and seeing through each one, passing through each one — then this is your true good spiritual friend, and right here and now you ascend to the unsurpassed Dharma gate of unobstructed, self-mastering, great liberation. Apart from this, what other good spiritual friend is there to visit? What other wondrous Dharma gate is there to enter?!

Now, to say nothing of the Dharma gates, even of good spiritual friends, how could there be as many as the motes of dust in the Buddha-lands — so very many? Little do people realize that what is called "in every mote of dust and every land" refers to the deluded thoughts, cogitations, and emotional defilements of our own daily life. If, in daily life, at the place where thoughts arise, where the roots of passion are firmly knotted, where love and hate intertwine and are hard to untangle, and where the various habits of greed, anger, folly, and pride are hard to wear away — if right there, at the fundamental point of pain, you thrust an awl, piercing through and seeing through each one
(as a dream, an illusion)
, passing through each one
(cutting off deluded thoughts)

. Then this is your true great good spiritual friend, and right here and now you attain the unsurpassed Dharma gate of unobstructed, self-mastering, great liberation. Apart from this, what other good spiritual friend is there to visit? What other wondrous Dharma gate is there to enter?
